explain.say: What is on your table every day, cheap and simple? Salt! In 1930, Mahatma Gandhi turned salt into a powerful protest against British rule in India. The board asks: why salt, of all things? Let's find out.

explain.say: Now the timeline. On 12 March 1930, Gandhi and 78 followers walked about 390 kilometres, for 24 days, to Dandi on the coast. On 6 April he picked up a lump of natural salt, breaking the law. How far is 390 kilometres from your home?

faq.a: Everyone needs salt to stay healthy, especially in hot weather when you sweat. Because rich and poor alike used it, a salt tax affected every family in India.

faq.q: What was the British salt law?
faq.a: The Salt Act of 1882 gave the British government control of salt. Indians could not collect or sell salt, and had to buy taxed salt instead.
Satyagraha means holding firmly to truth. It was Gandhi's method of nonviolent resistance: breaking unjust laws peacefully, refusing to hit back, and accepting punishment.

faq.q: How did the world hear about the Salt March?
faq.a: Newspaper and newsreel reporters from many countries followed it. The American reporter Webb Miller described peaceful protesters being beaten at Dharasana, shocking readers worldwide.
asks: Why did the Salt March become famous?

faq.a: On the morning of 6 April 1930, Gandhi reached the beach at Dandi in Gujarat and picked up a lump of natural salt, breaking the salt law as a symbol.
asks: Where did the Salt March end?

facts: The Salt March went from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, about 390 kilometres, from 12 March to 6 April 1930.
More than 60,000 people were arrested during the salt satyagraha.
Gandhi began the march with 78 followers.
